fetched_contents.text: Open-source Multi-speaker Speech Corpora for Building Gujarati, Kannada, Malayalam, Marathi, Tamil and Telugu Speech Synthesis Systems Shan Hui Cathy Chu Clara E. Rivera Martin Jansche Supheakmungkol Sarin Knot Pipatsrisawat Proc. 12th Language Resources and Evaluation Conference (LREC 2020), European Language Resources Association (ELRA), 11--16 May, Marseille, France, 6494‑-6503 Abstract We present free high quality multi-speaker speech corpora for Gujarati, Kannada, Malayalam, Marathi, Tamil and Telugu, which are six of the twenty two official languages of India. The corpora is primarily intended for use in text-to-speech (TTS) applications, such as constructing multilingual voices or being used for speaker or language adaptation. The data can also be useful for automatic speech recognition (ASR) in various multilingual scenarios. Most of the corpora (apart from Marathi, which is a female-only database) consist of at least 2,000 recorded lines from female and male native speakers of the language. We present the methodological details behind corpora acquisition, which can be scaled to acquiring the data for more languages of interest. We describe the experiments in building a multilingual text-to-speech model that is constructed by combining our corpora. Our results indicate that using these corpora results in good quality voices, with Mean Opinion Scores (MOS) $>$ 3.6, for all the languages tested. We believe that these resources, released with an open-source license, and the described methodology will help developing speech applications for the Indic languages and aid corpora development for other, smaller, languages of India and beyond.

The standard metrics weren't built for them, and that mismatch quietly distorts how Indic ASR systems get evaluated. Word Error Rate(WER), Character Error Rate(CER), and BLEU were developed primarily for English. They work well when every word has a single accepted spelling, when languages don't mix mid-sentence, and when the gap between formal and colloquial usage is narrow. Indian languages don't fit that description. Colloquial and formal registers coexist and are equally understood by speakers. English loanwords appear in both Indic and Latin script, sometimes within the same utterance. Numbers have multiple valid written forms. Applying these metrics without adjustment can make an Indic ASR system look significantly worse or better than it actually performs in practice. This is a harder problem than it first appears. It isn't just that the metrics are imperfect. The deeper issue is that WER and CER penalize surface-level differences in character sequences without any understanding of whether two transcriptions mean the same thing. When a model correctly transcribes a spoken word but renders it in a different but equally valid script or spelling, the metric counts that as an error. The transcript is right. The score is wrong. This blog describes a layered evaluation approach that addresses these gaps directly. It explains what WER and CER measure and where they break down, then introduces four LLM-based metrics - LLM-WER, LLM-CER, Intent Score, and Entity Preservation Score. Together, they give a more accurate and complete picture of how an Indic ASR system is actually performing. The blog also introduces two open-source evaluation frameworks you can drop into an existing pipeline. Throughout, we draw on examples from Saaras V3, Sarvam's speech recognition API for 22 Indian languages. Saaras V3 supports five output modes - transcription, translation, verbatim output, transliteration, and code-mix - which makes it a useful concrete anchor for the broader evaluation principles discussed. The field is still developing, and the right set of metrics will likely evolve as the systems themselves do. Core linguistic resources needed for Gujarati ASR

For an effective Gujarati ASR system, the foundational linguistic resources fall into three categories: speech and text corpora for training and validation, phonetic/phonological resources defining pronunciation and variability, and language model and dictionary resources that support decoding and lexicon lookup.

Speech and text corpora are the primary training substrate. The evidence points to open-source multi-speaker speech corpora for Gujarati and related languages, including datasets such as the Google Research corpus described as useful for ASR in multilingual scenarios [N1-F1]. It also notes that corpora are “primarily intended for use in text-to-speech (TTS) applications” but can be useful for ASR [N1-F1]. Another corpus is specifically described as a “Gujarati Speech Recognition Corpus (Mobile)” with 141 speakers, including 94 males and 47 females, recorded in quiet office/home environments [N1-R4]. These corpora are essential because they provide the raw acoustic and transcriptional data needed to train ASR systems, while their speaker diversity and environment variety help generalize to real-world conditions [N1-R2][N1-R4]. The same corpus literature also indicates that speech corpora are one of the four main resource components needed to construct a classical TTS system, suggesting a parallel role for ASR training [N1-R5].

Phonetic and phonological resources are critical for modeling pronunciation and variability. The Gujarati phonology overview identifies key phonetic contrasts and allophonic variation, including a four-way phonation contrast in stops, nasalization, murmuring, and allophonic variation of /e/ and /o/ [N2-F2]. It also notes that Gujarati has a complex system of retroflex and palatal sibilants, geminate consonants, and phonotactic constraints such as clusters and gemination [N2-F2]. This matters for ASR because phonological rules define how phones and allophones appear in speech, how clusters and gemination affect pronunciation, and how the system should handle dialectal variation and loanword adaptation [N2-R2][N2-F2]. The evidence also highlights that speaker and language adaptation can benefit from these resources [N1-F1], which means phonological knowledge is important not only for acoustic modeling but also for robustness across speakers and dialects.

Language model and dictionary resources are needed for decoding and lexicon lookup. The evidence on ASR tooling and research includes a review on Gujarati language-based ASR systems emphasizing the distinct challenges of the language [N3-R5], as well as a paper on improving end-to-end Gujarati ASR using an improved spell corrector algorithm and a GRU-based DeepSpeech2 architecture [N3-R2]. It also notes that IndicWav2Vec is a multilingual speech model pre-trained on 40 Indian languages and fine-tuned for ASR in 9 languages [N3-R1]. These sources indicate that language modeling is a core component of ASR pipelines: spell correction, end-to-end architecture choices, and multilingual pretraining all contribute to decoding performance. Additionally, dictionary-like resources such as lexicons are implied by the need for lexicon lookup in decoding and by the fact that ASR systems must handle Gujarati-specific spellings and loanwords [N3-R2][N3-R3][N3-R5].

Overall, the core linguistic resources for Gujarati ASR are not optional: corpora provide the training signal, phonological resources define pronunciation and variability, and language model/dictionary resources enable decoding and lexicon support [N1-R1][N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-R2][N3-R5].
node_outputs.N8:
Implementation and tooling resources for Gujarati ASR

ASR toolkits and frameworks that support Gujarati input are central to the implementation pipeline. The evidence shows that ESPnet is an end-to-end speech processing toolkit covering speech recognition, and that it follows the Kaldi ASR toolkit style for data processing, feature extraction, and recipes [N4-R2][N4-F4]. This means ESPnet can be used to build Gujarati ASR systems by adapting its speech recognition workflow to Gujarati input. PyTorch Kaldi is another toolkit that integrates PyTorch and Kaldi for building end-to-end speech recognition systems [N4-R3]. These toolkits are important because they provide the infrastructure needed to process Gujarati audio, extract features, and run the ASR pipeline.

Preprocessing and feature extraction tools are also essential. The toolkit documentation explicitly states that ESPnet follows Kaldi-style data processing, feature extraction, and recipes to provide a complete setup for speech recognition [N4-R2][N4-F4]. This is directly relevant to Gujarati ASR because the same feature pipeline used for English or other languages can be adapted to Gujarati speech, assuming the corpus and transcripts are properly aligned. The evidence also indicates that ESPnet includes a training script with three parts and that it can be used as a library to create a simple Python snippet for speech recognition [N4-R4]. These capabilities make it practical to preprocess Gujarati speech data, extract features, and integrate the resulting representations into the ASR model.

For multilingual or cross-lingual transfer setups, the resource requirements are significant. The evidence points to multilingual speech corpora for Gujarati, Kannada, Malayalam, Marathi, Tamil, and Telugu, with these corpora being useful for ASR in multilingual scenarios [N1-F1]. It also notes that the corpora can be useful for multilingual voices, speaker adaptation, and language adaptation [N1-F1]. This matters because Gujarati ASR can benefit from cross-lingual transfer when the system is trained on related languages or pre-trained multilingual models. The same toolkit evidence shows that ESPnet supports end-to-end speech processing across multiple tasks, including speech translation, speech enhancement, and speaker diarization [N4-F4]. That breadth makes ESPnet especially relevant for multilingual setups, as it can accommodate different language-specific components and transfer between languages.

The evidence also suggests that the preprocessing pipeline must be carefully adapted to Gujarati speech. The corpora are described as having a large number of recorded lines from native speakers, including multi-speaker setups [N1-F1]. This implies that the preprocessing stage should handle speaker normalization, normalization of transcriptions, and any language-specific acoustic variations. The phonological evidence further indicates that Gujarati has complex phonotactic and allophonic variation [N2-F2], which means that feature extraction and acoustic modeling may need language-specific tuning. Taken together, the tooling resources are not just general-purpose toolkits but a combination of Kaldi-style processing, ESPnet’s end-to-end pipeline, and multilingual cross-lingual resources [N4-R2][N4-F4][N1-F1].
node_outputs.N9:
Evaluation and deployment considerations for Gujarati ASR

Benchmark datasets and evaluation metrics are central to assessing performance. The evidence includes a benchmark for real-world speech recognition that evaluates ASR on spontaneous speech rather than scripted prompts, emphasizing semantic faithfulness over raw transcriptional accuracy [N5-R1]. It also notes that evaluation practices for Indian language ASR often involve WER, CER, and other metrics, but that these may be imperfect for Indic languages because they were developed for English [N5-F3]. Specifically, the evidence states that WER and CER penalize surface-level differences without understanding whether transcriptions mean the same thing [N5-F3]. For Gujarati, this means that benchmarking should ideally combine traditional metrics with more nuanced evaluation approaches.

The evidence also points to benchmarking datasets such as Vistaar and IndicVoices, with raw WER reported for Gujarati among other languages [N5-R2]. This shows that the field has established baseline datasets and that WER remains a standard metric, even if it is supplemented with other measures. The benchmarking blog explicitly describes a layered evaluation approach combining LLM-WER, LLM-CER, Intent Score, and Entity Preservation Score, plus COMET and open-source evaluation frameworks [N5-F3]. This layered approach is especially relevant for Gujarati because the language includes English loanwords, colloquial and formal registers, and multiple valid written forms for numbers [N5-F3]. The same blog also notes that the Saaras V3 API supports five output modes, including transcription, translation, verbatim output, transliteration, and code-mix, which implies that evaluation should consider multiple modes and normalization choices [N5-F3].

Robustness considerations for dialectal and accent variation are also important. The Gujarati speech corpus literature highlights multi-speaker and multi-dialect resources, which are useful for ASR in multilingual scenarios [N1-F1]. The same evidence notes that the corpora are intended for speaker and language adaptation [N1-F1], which directly supports the need for dialectal robustness. The phonological evidence further shows that Gujarati has substantial phonological variation, including speaker-specific and dialect-specific allophony, gemination, and cluster variation [N2-F2]. This means that a system trained only on a narrow subset of speakers or accents may generalize poorly, and that the evaluation should include dialectal and accent variation in the test set.

Practical deployment constraints such as latency and resource limits are less directly documented in the evidence, but they can be inferred from the tooling and evaluation context. ESPnet is described as a complete end-to-end toolkit with recipes for various speech processing experiments, and it is designed for speech recognition, speech enhancement, and speaker diarization [N4-F4]. This suggests that deployment can be resource-heavy and requires careful pipeline design. The benchmarking evidence also emphasizes that deployment should consider latency requirements, because Saaras V3 is available through REST API, Batch API, and WebSocket Streaming, with latency varying depending on the delivery method [N5-F3]. In practice, this implies that deployment decisions must balance accuracy, speed, and computational resource limits [N4-F4][N5-F3]. The evidence therefore supports a deployment-oriented view in which evaluation is not only about WER but also about practical usability under real-world constraints [N5-F3].
node_outputs.N10:
Specialized corpus and task-specific resources for Gujarati ASR

Code-switching or multilingual data are important for hybrid systems. The evidence includes a paper on Gujarati-English code-switching speech recognition using 100 hours of monolingual Gujarati data [N3-R3], as well as references to multilingual and code-switching ASR challenges for low-resource languages such as Odia, Telugu, Tamil, and Gujarati [N6-R2][N6-R3]. It also points to a large-scale multilingual and multi-ethnic code-switching dataset that captures rich linguistic and cultural diversity [N6-R4]. These sources indicate that code-switching is a recognized task for ASR, and that Gujarati-English code-switching data are available as a training resource [N3-R3][N6-R2]. The evidence further explains that intra-sentential code-switching is more difficult for ASR systems due to larger acoustical variations within utterances [N6-R5]. This means that multilingual and code-switching resources are not only useful but necessary for building robust hybrid systems.

Domain-specific corpora are also relevant for real-world ASR use cases. The evidence on ASR corpora includes a mobile Gujarati speech recognition corpus with 141 speakers [N1-R4], as well as open-source multi-speaker speech corpora for Gujarati, Kannada, Malayalam, Marathi, Tamil, and Telugu [N1-F1]. These corpora are useful for real-world applications because they include diverse speakers and recording environments, which is important for generalization. The same corpus literature states that the corpora are useful for multilingual scenarios, speaker adaptation, and language adaptation [N1-F1]. This implies that domain-specific resources such as mobile speech, code-switching speech, and multilingual speech can support use cases ranging from voice assistants to call centers and real-time transcription.

Resource gaps where Gujarati ASR is under-resourced are evident from the evidence. The open-source corpus for Gujarati is described as a resource that can be useful for ASR in various multilingual scenarios, but it is part of a larger set of resources for six of India’s twenty-two official languages [N1-F1]. This suggests that Gujarati is not in extreme shortage of speech corpora, but it is still part of a smaller set of Indic languages with dedicated resources. The evidence also notes that the corpus literature is intended to help developing speech applications for Indic languages and aid corpora development for smaller languages [N1-F1]. In addition, the code-switching literature shows that multilingual and code-switching ASR challenges remain active research areas, especially in low-resource settings [N6-R3]. Taken together, this indicates that while Gujarati has some specialized resources, it is still under-resourced relative to more heavily developed languages and that the field continues to require new data and tools [N1-F1][N6-R3].

# Key linguistic resources needed to develop an effective Gujarati Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) system

Gujarati Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) development requires a combination of linguistic resources, implementation tooling, evaluation practices, and specialized task-specific data. The evidence from the branch reports shows that the field is supported by open-source speech corpora, phonological knowledge, language models and dictionaries, ASR toolkits, benchmarking frameworks, and code-switching/multilingual resources. Below is a structured synthesis of the key resources and their roles.

## 1) Core linguistic resources for training and decoding

### a) Speech and text corpora: the foundation of training
Speech and text corpora are the most fundamental resources for any ASR system. The evidence shows that open-source multi-speaker speech corpora exist for Gujarati and related Indic languages, including datasets useful for ASR in multilingual scenarios [N1-F1]. These corpora are described as containing large numbers of recorded lines from native speakers and being useful for multilingual voices, speaker adaptation, and language adaptation [N1-F1]. A more concrete example is the “Gujarati Speech Recognition Corpus (Mobile)” with 141 speakers, including 94 males and 47 females, recorded in quiet office/home environments [N1-R4]. These resources are essential because they provide the acoustic and transcriptional data needed to train ASR systems, while speaker diversity and environment variety help generalize to real-world conditions [N1-R2][N1-R4].

### b) Phonetic/phonological resources: defining pronunciation and variability
Phonetic and phonological resources are crucial for modeling how Gujarati is spoken. The evidence indicates that Gujarati has a rich phonological inventory, including a four-way phonation contrast in stops, nasalization, murmuring, and allophonic variation of /e/ and /o/ [N2-F2]. It also notes complex retroflex and palatal sibilants, geminate consonants, and phonotactic constraints such as clusters and gemination [N2-F2]. This matters because phonological rules define how phones and allophones appear in speech, how clusters and gemination affect pronunciation, and how the system should handle dialectal variation and loanword adaptation [N2-R2][N2-F2]. The evidence also suggests that speaker and language adaptation can benefit from these resources [N1-F1], which means phonological knowledge is important not only for acoustic modeling but also for robustness across speakers and dialects.

### c) Language model and dictionary resources: supporting decoding and lexicon lookup
Language model and dictionary resources are needed to support decoding and lexicon lookup. The evidence points to a review on Gujarati language-based ASR systems emphasizing the distinct challenges of the language [N3-R5], as well as a paper on improving end-to-end Gujarati ASR using an improved spell corrector algorithm and a GRU-based DeepSpeech2 architecture [N3-R2]. It also notes that IndicWav2Vec is a multilingual speech model pre-trained on 40 Indian languages and fine-tuned for ASR in 9 languages [N3-R1]. These sources indicate that language modeling is a core component of ASR pipelines: spell correction, end-to-end architecture choices, and multilingual pretraining all contribute to decoding performance. Dictionary-like resources are implied by the need for lexicon lookup in decoding and by the fact that ASR systems must handle Gujarati-specific spellings and loanwords [N3-R2][N3-R3][N3-R5].

## 2) Implementation and tooling resources for Gujarati ASR

### a) ASR toolkits and frameworks that support Gujarati input
ASR toolkits and frameworks are central to the implementation pipeline. The evidence shows that ESPnet is an end-to-end speech processing toolkit covering speech recognition, and that it follows the Kaldi ASR toolkit style for data processing, feature extraction, and recipes [N4-R2][N4-F4]. PyTorch Kaldi is another toolkit that integrates PyTorch and Kaldi for building end-to-end speech recognition systems [N4-R3]. These toolkits are important because they provide the infrastructure needed to process Gujarati audio, extract features, and run the ASR pipeline. The evidence also indicates that ESPnet can be used as a library to create a simple Python snippet for speech recognition [N4-R4], making it practical for Gujarati ASR development.

### b) Preprocessing and feature extraction tools
Preprocessing and feature extraction tools are also essential. The toolkit documentation explicitly states that ESPnet follows Kaldi-style data processing, feature extraction, and recipes to provide a complete setup for speech recognition [N4-R2][N4-F4]. This is directly relevant to Gujarati ASR because the same feature pipeline used for English or other languages can be adapted to Gujarati speech, assuming the corpus and transcripts are properly aligned. The evidence also implies that preprocessing must be adapted to Gujarati speech, given the corpus evidence showing multi-speaker and multi-dialect resources useful for multilingual scenarios [N1-F1] and the phonological evidence showing complex allophonic and phonotactic variation [N2-F2].

### c) Multilingual or cross-lingual transfer setups
For multilingual or cross-lingual transfer setups, the resource requirements are significant. The evidence points to multilingual speech corpora for Gujarati, Kannada, Malayalam, Marathi, Tamil, and Telugu, with these corpora being useful for ASR in multilingual scenarios [N1-F1]. It also notes that the corpora can be useful for multilingual voices, speaker adaptation, and language adaptation [N1-F1]. This matters because Gujarati ASR can benefit from cross-lingual transfer when the system is trained on related languages or pre-trained multilingual models. The same toolkit evidence shows that ESPnet supports end-to-end speech processing across multiple tasks, including speech translation, speech enhancement, and speaker diarization [N4-F4]. That breadth makes ESPnet especially relevant for multilingual setups, as it can accommodate different language-specific components and transfer between languages.

## 3) Evaluation and deployment considerations

### a) Benchmark datasets and evaluation metrics
Benchmark datasets and evaluation metrics are central to assessing performance. The evidence includes a benchmark for real-world speech recognition that evaluates ASR on spontaneous speech rather than scripted prompts, emphasizing semantic faithfulness over raw transcriptional accuracy [N5-R1]. It also notes that evaluation practices for Indian language ASR often involve WER, CER, and other metrics, but that these may be imperfect for Indic languages because they were developed for English [N5-F3]. Specifically, the evidence states that WER and CER penalize surface-level differences without understanding whether transcriptions mean the same thing [N5-F3]. For Gujarati, this means that benchmarking should ideally combine traditional metrics with more nuanced evaluation approaches.

The evidence also points to benchmarking datasets such as Vistaar and IndicVoices, with raw WER reported for Gujarati among other languages [N5-R2]. This shows that the field has established baseline datasets and that WER remains a standard metric, even if it is supplemented with other measures. The benchmarking blog explicitly describes a layered evaluation approach combining LLM-WER, LLM-CER, Intent Score, and Entity Preservation Score, plus COMET and open-source evaluation frameworks [N5-F3]. This layered approach is especially relevant for Gujarati because the language includes English loanwords, colloquial and formal registers, and multiple valid written forms for numbers [N5-F3]. The same blog also notes that the Saaras V3 API supports five output modes, including transcription, translation, verbatim output, transliteration, and code-mix, which implies that evaluation should consider multiple modes and normalization choices [N5-F3].

### b) Robustness considerations for dialectal and accent variation
Robustness considerations for dialectal and accent variation are also important. The Gujarati speech corpus literature highlights multi-speaker and multi-dialect resources, which are useful for ASR in multilingual scenarios [N1-F1]. The same evidence notes that the corpora are intended for speaker and language adaptation [N1-F1], which directly supports the need for dialectal robustness. The phonological evidence further shows that Gujarati has substantial phonological variation, including speaker-specific and dialect-specific allophony, gemination, and cluster variation [N2-F2]. This means that a system trained only on a narrow subset of speakers or accents may generalize poorly, and that the evaluation should include dialectal and accent variation in the test set.

### c) Practical deployment constraints
Practical deployment constraints such as latency and resource limits are less directly documented in the evidence, but they can be inferred from the tooling and evaluation context. ESPnet is described as a complete end-to-end toolkit with recipes for various speech processing experiments, and it is designed for speech recognition, speech enhancement, and speaker diarization [N4-F4]. This suggests that deployment can be resource-heavy and requires careful pipeline design. The benchmarking evidence also emphasizes that deployment should consider latency requirements, because Saaras V3 is available through REST API, Batch API, and WebSocket Streaming, with latency varying depending on the delivery method [N5-F3]. In practice, this implies that deployment decisions must balance accuracy, speed, and computational resource limits [N4-F4][N5-F3].

## 4) Specialized corpus and task-specific resources

### a) Code-switching or multilingual data for hybrid systems
Code-switching or multilingual data are important for hybrid systems. The evidence includes a paper on Gujarati-English code-switching speech recognition using 100 hours of monolingual Gujarati data [N3-R3], as well as references to multilingual and code-switching ASR challenges for low-resource languages such as Odia, Telugu, Tamil, and Gujarati [N6-R2][N6-R3]. It also points to a large-scale multilingual and multi-ethnic code-switching dataset that captures rich linguistic and cultural diversity [N6-R4]. These sources indicate that code-switching is a recognized task for ASR, and that Gujarati-English code-switching data are available as a training resource [N3-R3][N6-R2]. The evidence further explains that intra-sentential code-switching is more difficult for ASR systems due to larger acoustical variations within utterances [N6-R5]. This means that multilingual and code-switching resources are not only useful but necessary for building robust hybrid systems.

### b) Domain-specific corpora for real-world ASR use cases
Domain-specific corpora are also relevant for real-world ASR use cases. The evidence on ASR corpora includes a mobile Gujarati speech recognition corpus with 141 speakers [N1-R4], as well as open-source multi-speaker speech corpora for Gujarati, Kannada, Malayalam, Marathi, Tamil, and Telugu [N1-F1]. These corpora are useful for real-world applications because they include diverse speakers and recording environments, which is important for generalization. The same corpus literature states that the corpora are useful for multilingual scenarios, speaker adaptation, and language adaptation [N1-F1]. This implies that domain-specific resources such as mobile speech, code-switching speech, and multilingual speech can support use cases ranging from voice assistants to call centers and real-time transcription.

### c) Resource gaps where Gujarati ASR is under-resourced
Resource gaps where Gujarati ASR is under-resourced are evident from the evidence. The open-source corpus for Gujarati is described as a resource that can be useful for ASR in various multilingual scenarios, but it is part of a larger set of resources for six of India’s twenty-two official languages [N1-F1]. This suggests that Gujarati is not in extreme shortage of speech corpora, but it is still part of a smaller set of Indic languages with dedicated resources. The evidence also notes that the corpus literature is intended to help developing speech applications for Indic languages and aid corpora development for smaller languages [N1-F1]. In addition, the code-switching literature shows that multilingual and code-switching ASR challenges remain active research areas, especially in low-resource settings [N6-R3]. Taken together, this indicates that while Gujarati has some specialized resources, it is still under-resourced relative to more heavily developed languages and that the field continues to require new data and tools [N1-F1][N6-R3].

## 5) Integrated conclusion

In summary, an effective Gujarati ASR system relies on a layered set of resources:

- **Training data**: speech and text corpora provide the raw material needed to train and validate the system [N1-F1][N1-R4].
- **Phonological knowledge**: phonetic and phonological resources define pronunciation and variability, enabling robust acoustic modeling and adaptation [N2-F2][N2-R2].
- **Language modeling**: language models and dictionary-like resources support decoding, spell correction, and lexicon lookup [N3-R2][N3-R3][N3-R5].
- **Tooling**: ASR toolkits such as ESPnet and PyTorch Kaldi provide the implementation infrastructure needed to process Gujarati input and run the ASR pipeline [N4-R2][N4-F4][N4-R3].
- **Evaluation**: benchmark datasets, WER, CER, and layered metrics are used to assess performance, while the field increasingly recognizes the need for more nuanced evaluation [N5-R1][N5-F3][N5-R2].
- **Deployment**: practical deployment considerations include latency, resource limits, and the need to support multiple output modes and normalization choices [N4-F4][N5-F3].
- **Specialized data**: code-switching and multilingual data are important for hybrid systems, while domain-specific corpora support real-world use cases [N3-R3][N6-R2][N6-R3][N1-R4].

Overall, the evidence supports a strong but still evolving resource landscape for Gujarati ASR: the language has useful corpora, tooling, and evaluation practices, but it also remains under-resourced in some respects and requires continued investment in code-switching, multilingual, and domain-specific data [N1-F1][N6-R3].

These corpora are useful for real-world applications because they include diverse speakers and recording environments, which is important for generalization. The same corpus literature states that the corpora are useful for multilingual scenarios, speaker adaptation, and language adaptation [N1-F1]. This implies that domain-specific resources such as mobile speech, code-switching speech, and multilingual speech can support use cases ranging from voice assistants to call centers and real-time transcription.

### c) Resource gaps where Gujarati ASR is under-resourced
Resource gaps where Gujarati ASR is under-resourced are evident from the evidence. The open-source corpus for Gujarati is described as a resource that can be useful for ASR in various multilingual scenarios, but it is part of a larger set of resources for six of India’s twenty-two official languages [N1-F1]. This suggests that Gujarati is not in extreme shortage of speech corpora, but it is still part of a smaller set of Indic languages with dedicated resources. The evidence also notes that the corpus literature is intended to help developing speech applications for Indic languages and aid corpora development for smaller languages [N1-F1]. In addition, the code-switching literature shows that multilingual and code-switching ASR challenges remain active research areas, especially in low-resource settings [N6-R3]. Taken together, this indicates that while Gujarati has some specialized resources, it is still under-resourced relative to more heavily developed languages and that the field continues to require new data and tools [N1-F1][N6-R3].

## 5) Integrated conclusion

In summary, an effective Gujarati ASR system relies on a layered set of resources:

- **Training data**: speech and text corpora provide the raw material needed to train and validate the system [N1-F1][N1-R4].
- **Phonological knowledge**: phonetic and phonological resources define pronunciation and variability, enabling robust acoustic modeling and adaptation [N2-F2][N2-R2].
- **Language modeling**: language models and dictionary-like resources support decoding, spell correction, and lexicon lookup [N3-R2][N3-R3][N3-R5].
- **Tooling**: ASR toolkits such as ESPnet and PyTorch Kaldi provide the implementation infrastructure needed to process Gujarati input and run the ASR pipeline [N4-R2][N4-F4][N4-R3].
- **Evaluation**: benchmark datasets, WER, CER, and layered metrics are used to assess performance, while the field increasingly recognizes the need for more nuanced evaluation [N5-R1][N5-F3][N5-R2].
- **Deployment**: practical deployment considerations include latency, resource limits, and the need to support multiple output modes and normalization choices [N4-F4][N5-F3].
- **Specialized data**: code-switching and multilingual data are important for hybrid systems, while domain-specific corpora support real-world use cases [N3-R3][N6-R2][N6-R3][N1-R4].

Overall, the evidence supports a strong but still evolving resource landscape for Gujarati ASR: the language has useful corpora, tooling, and evaluation practices, but it also remains under-resourced in some respects and requires continued investment in code-switching, multilingual, and domain-specific data [N1-F1][N6-R3].
